ev.ane_h_hyksos.fight.success: Avaris fell. You came home with a share of the spoils.
ev.ane_h_hyksos.fight.failure: An arrow struck you beneath the walls of Avaris.
ev.ane_h_hyksos.title: The Hyksos driven out
ev.ane_h_hyksos.text: King Ahmose has laid siege to Avaris, the Delta capital of the foreign Hyksos rulers. Barges full of troops are leaving Thebes, and every village must give grain and men.
ev.ane_h_hyksos.note: Around 1550–1540 BC the Theban king Ahmose I took Avaris and expelled the Hyksos, who had ruled Lower Egypt for about a century. His reign is counted as the start of the New Kingdom. The exact years are debated.
ev.ane_h_kassite_marduk.title: Marduk returns
ev.ane_h_kassite_marduk.text: The Kassite king Agum has announced that he has brought back to Babylon the statue of Marduk carried off by foreigners many years ago. It is being dressed again in gold and gems, and the whole city goes to Esagila.
ev.ane_h_kassite_marduk.note: After the Hittite sack of Babylon (around 1595 BC) the statue of Marduk was taken abroad. Its return by the Kassite king Agum II is known from an inscription surviving only in a late copy; its authenticity and dating are disputed.
ev.ane_h_assur_border.title: A border by oath
ev.ane_h_assur_border.text: The kings of Assur and Babylon have sworn oaths to each other and fixed the border between their lands. The merchants are delighted: the roads south and north are open again.
ev.ane_h_assur_border.note: The Assyrian "Synchronistic History" records that Puzur-Ashur III and the Kassite king Burna-Buriash I made a border treaty. It is one of the few sources on the early Kassite period; the dates are approximate.
ev.ane_h_deir_el_medina.gossip: Wonder what they hide in the cliffs
ev.ane_h_deir_el_medina.title: Hidden tombs
ev.ane_h_deir_el_medina.text: They say the king has ordered his tomb cut not in a pyramid but deep in the cliffs of a desert valley on the west bank. The craftsmen are housed apart, in a new village, and forbidden to speak of their work.
ev.ane_h_deir_el_medina.note: Thutmose I was apparently the first pharaoh to be buried in the Valley of the Kings. The workmen's village of Deir el-Medina, home to the royal tomb builders for nearly 500 years, was probably founded in his reign.
ev.ane_h_sealand.go.success: The Sealand submitted, and you came home with spoils.
ev.ane_h_sealand.go.failure: Marsh fever laid you low before the first battle.
ev.ane_h_sealand.title: War on the Sealand
ev.ane_h_sealand.text: The Kassite king is leading his army south into the marshy Sealand, which has long had kings of its own. They say that after victory the whole south down to the sea will belong to Babylon.
ev.ane_h_sealand.note: Around the mid-15th century BC the Kassites conquered the "Sealand Dynasty" in the far south of Mesopotamia and united Babylonia. Details and the exact date are unknown.
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut.approve: The gods know whom to choose
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut.doubt: Grumble that it is not proper
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut.title: A woman as Pharaoh
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut.text: Hatshepsut, widow of the late king and regent for the boy Thutmose, has taken the full royal titles. Her new statues show her with a beard and the royal headcloth.
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut.note: Hatshepsut ruled around 1479–1458 BC, first as regent for Thutmose III, then as pharaoh. Her reign was a time of peace, building and trading expeditions.
ev.ane_h_punt.incense: Buy a pinch of myrrh for the house
ev.ane_h_punt.title: Ships from Punt
ev.ane_h_punt.text: The queen's expedition to the distant land of Punt has returned: the ships brought live myrrh trees in baskets, incense, ebony, gold and monkeys. The trees will be planted at Hatshepsut's temple.
ev.ane_h_punt.note: The expedition to Punt (probably on the Red Sea coast south of Egypt) in Hatshepsut's year 9 is depicted on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahari.
ev.ane_h_megiddo.march.success: Megiddo surrendered, and you got a share of the spoils.
ev.ane_h_megiddo.march.failure: You lay wounded in the camp beneath the walls.
ev.ane_h_megiddo.title: Megiddo
ev.ane_h_megiddo.text: Thutmose III has led the army into Canaan against an alliance of princes headed by the ruler of Kadesh. They say he chose a narrow mountain pass that no one expected and came out right at Megiddo.
ev.ane_h_megiddo.note: The battle of Megiddo in Thutmose III's year 23 is described in his annals at Karnak; the city surrendered after a seven-month siege. The year is around 1457 BC (other reckonings give 1479 or 1482).
ev.ane_h_mitanni_assur.hide.failure: The tribute collectors found the hiding place.
ev.ane_h_mitanni_assur.title: Tribute to Mitanni
ev.ane_h_mitanni_assur.text: The army of the king of Mitanni has entered Assur. They took the temple doors, plated with silver and gold, and carried them off to their capital. The city now pays tribute to the Hurrian king.
ev.ane_h_mitanni_assur.note: Around the mid-15th century BC Saushtatar of Mitanni subdued Assur and, according to a later document, carried silver and gold doors from it to Washukanni. Assyria remained subject for almost a century.
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut_erased.remember: Tell the children what she was like
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut_erased.title: An erased name
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut_erased.text: In the temples stonecutters are chiselling Queen Hatshepsut's images and name from the walls, and her statues are broken and thrown into a pit. The old folk whisper, but nobody says a word aloud.
ev.ane_h_hatshepsut_erased.note: Towards the end of Thutmose III's reign, more than 20 years after Hatshepsut's death, her monuments began to be destroyed. The reasons are debated: perhaps it concerned his son's claim to the throne rather than personal revenge.
ev.ane_h_dur_kurigalzu.title: The city of Kurigalzu
ev.ane_h_dur_kurigalzu.text: King Kurigalzu is building a new city north of Babylon bearing his name: a palace, temples and a huge ziggurat of mud brick layered with reed mats. Brickmakers and porters are being hired.
ev.ane_h_dur_kurigalzu.note: Dur-Kurigalzu (modern Aqar Quf) was founded by the Kassite king Kurigalzu I around the 1390s BC. The remains of its ziggurat, about 50 m high, still stand.
ev.ane_h_amarna_letters.listen: Listen to the news at market
ev.ane_h_amarna_letters.title: Pharaoh's gold
ev.ane_h_amarna_letters.text: The envoys are back from Egypt. The king is displeased: twenty minas of gold yielded not even five after smelting, and he is writing Pharaoh an angry letter. Meanwhile merchants say their caravan was robbed in Canaan.
ev.ane_h_amarna_letters.text.assur: King Ashur-uballit has sent envoys to Pharaoh and called himself a "great king" in his letter — the equal of the kings of Egypt, Babylon and Hatti. In Babylon, they say, people are very annoyed.
ev.ane_h_amarna_letters.note: The Amarna archive (around 1360–1335 BC) is a set of clay tablets holding the correspondence of the pharaohs with the kings of Babylon, Assyria, Mitanni and Hatti and the princes of Canaan. The Babylonian king Burna-Buriash II complained of poor gold and of robbed merchants; the Assyrian Ashur-uballit I addressed Pharaoh as an equal for the first time.
ev.ane_h_ashur_uballit.title: Free of Mitanni
ev.ane_h_ashur_uballit.text: Mitanni is weakened by wars and strife, and King Ashur-uballit has stopped paying it tribute. For the first time in a hundred years Assur answers to no one. In the market people speak of "the land of Ashur", not just a city.
ev.ane_h_ashur_uballit.note: Ashur-uballit I (around 1363–1328 BC) freed Assyria from Mitanni. The Middle Assyrian kingdom is counted from his reign.
ev.ane_h_amun_closed.title: The temples are closed
ev.ane_h_amun_closed.text: The temples of Amun and the other gods are being closed, and their lands and income go to the Aten. Festivals are cancelled, and priests and temple workers are left without rations. Even the word "gods" in the plural is avoided in writing now.
ev.ane_h_amun_closed.note: Around years 9–12 of Akhenaten's reign (roughly 1344–1340 BC) the old cults were closed and the name of Amun destroyed. How deeply the reform touched ordinary people is debated: amulets of Bes and Taweret turn up in the houses of Amarna itself.
ev.ane_h_plague.flee: Go to the countryside, away from people
ev.ane_h_plague.title: Pestilence
ev.ane_h_plague.text: A pestilence is going through the city: people burn up with fever in a few days. They say the sickness came with caravans and prisoners from Canaan. Some houses are burying one after another.
ev.ane_h_plague.note: Letters in the Amarna archive mention pestilence at Byblos and on Cyprus, and the Hittite king Mursili II in his prayers blames Egyptian prisoners for a long epidemic. Whether it struck Egypt itself, and what the disease was, is debated.
ev.ane_h_restoration.work: Hire on to restore the temple
ev.ane_h_restoration.title: The gods return
ev.ane_h_restoration.text: The young king Tutankhamun — formerly Tutankhaten — has given the temples back their lands and priests. A stela at Karnak says the land was in turmoil and the gods had turned their backs on Egypt. The Opet festival is celebrated again.
ev.ane_h_restoration.note: Tutankhamun's "Restoration Stela" (around 1334–1332 BC) describes the reinstatement of the old cults after the Amarna period. The court returned from Akhetaten to Memphis and Thebes.
ev.ane_h_kara_hardash.profit: Buy up grain while it is cheap
ev.ane_h_kara_hardash.title: A king murdered
ev.ane_h_kara_hardash.text: Kassite soldiers have mutinied and killed the young king of Babylon, Kara-hardash, grandson of the Assyrian king. Ashur-uballit is already marching south to take revenge and put his own man on the throne.
ev.ane_h_kara_hardash.note: Around 1333 BC Kara-hardash, son of an Assyrian princess, was killed in Babylon. Ashur-uballit I intervened and set Kurigalzu II on the throne. The sources are later chronicles that differ in detail.
ev.ane_h_tutankhamun_death.title: Death of the boy king
ev.ane_h_tutankhamun_death.text: King Tutankhamun has died, still a youth, leaving no children. He is being buried hastily in a small tomb in the Valley of the Kings, and the old official Ay takes the throne. The widowed queen, they say, is in despair.
ev.ane_h_tutankhamun_death.note: Tutankhamun died around 1327 BC at about 19. His tomb, almost untouched by robbers, was found in 1922. Hittite texts tell of a letter from a widowed Egyptian queen asking for a Hittite prince to marry.
ev.ane_h_horemheb_edict.complain.success: The collector was removed and your grain returned.
ev.ane_h_horemheb_edict.complain.failure: Your complaint was lost, and the collector now looks at you askance.
ev.ane_h_horemheb_edict.title: An edict against extortion
ev.ane_h_horemheb_edict.text: King Horemheb has had an edict read out: collectors who take boats, hides or vegetables from the poor beyond what is due will be severely punished. Judges are forbidden to accept gifts.
ev.ane_h_horemheb_edict.note: Horemheb's "Great Edict" (around 1320–1300 BC) survives on a stela at Karnak. It lists abuses by officials and soldiers and the penalties for them.
ev.ane_h_kurigalzu_elam.go.success: You came back from Elam with spoils.
ev.ane_h_kurigalzu_elam.go.failure: You came back with a wound and an empty sack.
ev.ane_h_kurigalzu_elam.stay: Watch the spoils arrive at the gate
ev.ane_h_kurigalzu_elam.title: Campaign against Elam
ev.ane_h_kurigalzu_elam.text: King Kurigalzu has defeated the Elamites and, they say, entered their city of Susa. Spoils are being brought to Babylon and victory offerings to the temples.
ev.ane_h_kurigalzu_elam.note: Kurigalzu II (around 1332–1308 BC) fought Elam and Assyria. Inscriptions naming Kurigalzu have been found at Susa, but which of the two kings of that name defeated Elam is debated.
ev.ane_h_pi_ramesses.title: A new capital in the Delta
ev.ane_h_pi_ramesses.text: Ramesses II is building a vast city in the eastern Delta: Pi-Ramesses, "House of Ramesses". The court, the army and the chariot workshops are moving there, and endless barges of stone and people pass through Memphis.
ev.ane_h_pi_ramesses.note: Pi-Ramesses, on the site of old Avaris, became the main residence of Ramesses II. Later, when its branch of the Nile silted up, its monuments were moved to Tanis.
ev.ane_h_kadesh.march.success: You survived that slaughter and came home a hero — at least in the stories.
ev.ane_h_kadesh.march.failure: Hittite chariots crushed your unit. You came home badly wounded.
ev.ane_h_kadesh.title: Kadesh
ev.ane_h_kadesh.text: Ramesses II has led four divisions — Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth — to Kadesh against the Hittite king Muwatalli. The news is contradictory: heralds proclaim a great victory, while returning soldiers say they barely escaped with their lives.
ev.ane_h_kadesh.note: The battle of Kadesh (around 1274 BC) was one of the largest chariot battles of antiquity. Ramesses portrayed it as his victory on the walls of many temples, but Kadesh remained in Hittite hands.
ev.ane_h_ramesseum.title: The works of Ramesses
ev.ane_h_ramesseum.text: On the west bank the memorial temple of Ramesses II rises with a colossus of solid granite, and at Karnak the giant hall of columns is being finished. There are never enough stonecutters, porters and scribes.
ev.ane_h_ramesseum.note: The Ramesseum and the Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak are among the largest works of Ramesses II (around 1279–1213 BC). Huge mud-brick granaries stood beside the Ramesseum.
ev.ane_h_hanigalbat.title: Lands in the west
ev.ane_h_hanigalbat.text: The kings of Assur have conquered Hanigalbat, the remnant of the kingdom of Mitanni. New lands beyond the Khabur river are being given to settlers: a house, a field and the duty to serve the king.
ev.ane_h_hanigalbat.note: Adad-nirari I (around 1305–1274 BC) and Shalmaneser I (around 1273–1244 BC) conquered Hanigalbat. The Assyrians deported conquered peoples on a large scale and planted their own settlers and forts on the new lands.
ev.ane_h_hittite_peace.trade: Invest in trade with the north
ev.ane_h_hittite_peace.title: Eternal peace with the Hittites
ev.ane_h_hittite_peace.text: The Hittite king's envoys have brought a silver tablet with a treaty: Egypt and Hatti swear eternal peace and mutual aid. There will be no more war in the north — if the gods allow.
ev.ane_h_hittite_peace.note: The treaty between Ramesses II and Hattusili III (around 1259 BC) survives in two versions — Egyptian on temple walls and Akkadian on tablets from the Hittite capital. It is one of the oldest known peace treaties.
ev.ane_h_babylon_sacked.hide.success: You were lucky: they took little.
ev.ane_h_babylon_sacked.fight.success: You survived and kept your people safe.
ev.ane_h_babylon_sacked.title: Babylon taken
ev.ane_h_babylon_sacked.text: The Assyrian king Tukulti-Ninurta has defeated the Babylonians, captured King Kashtiliash and entered the city. The Assyrians are looting the temples and carrying off the statue of Marduk and whole libraries of tablets.
ev.ane_h_babylon_sacked.text.assur: News has come: King Tukulti-Ninurta has taken Babylon and captured the Kassite king. Spoils, prisoners and the tablets of Babylonian scribes are being brought to Assur. Some rejoice; others fear the wrath of Marduk.
ev.ane_h_babylon_sacked.note: Around 1225 BC Tukulti-Ninurta I captured Babylon and ruled it through governors for several years. The victory is celebrated in the Assyrian "Tukulti-Ninurta Epic". The date is approximate.
ev.ane_h_tukulti_murder.gods: Admit that the gods see everything
ev.ane_h_tukulti_murder.title: The end of Tukulti-Ninurta
ev.ane_h_tukulti_murder.text: They say his son and the nobles shut King Tukulti-Ninurta up in his new city and killed him. The Babylonians whisper that it is Marduk's punishment for the plundered temple.
ev.ane_h_tukulti_murder.note: Tukulti-Ninurta I died around 1207 BC in a conspiracy, by the chronicle's account at the hands of his son Ashur-nadin-apli. Assyria was weakened for almost a century afterwards.
ev.ane_h_ramesses_dies.title: Ramesses is dead
ev.ane_h_ramesses_dies.text: Ramesses II has died after 66 years on the throne. Almost no one in the land remembers another king. He had so many children that many of his sons died before him; his thirteenth son, Merneptah, no longer young, takes the throne.
ev.ane_h_ramesses_dies.note: Ramesses II reigned around 1279–1213 BC and outlived twelve heirs. His mummy survives and is in Cairo.
ev.ane_h_libyans.fight.success: Victory! You came home with spoils.
ev.ane_h_libyans.fight.failure: You were wounded in the battle at Perire.
ev.ane_h_libyans.title: Libyans in the Delta
ev.ane_h_libyans.text: Libyans with their wives, children and cattle are moving into the Delta from the west, and with them northern "peoples of the sea". Merneptah is leading the army against them. People from the western villages are fleeing toward Memphis.
ev.ane_h_libyans.note: In Merneptah's year 5 (around 1208 BC) the Egyptians defeated the Libyans and their allies. The victory stela contains the first known mention of "Israel".
ev.ane_h_adad_shuma_usur.join.success: You were among those who drove out the Assyrians.
ev.ane_h_adad_shuma_usur.join.failure: You were wounded in a skirmish at the gate.
ev.ane_h_adad_shuma_usur.title: The Assyrians driven out
ev.ane_h_adad_shuma_usur.text: The Babylonian nobles have risen against the Assyrian governors and set the Kassite prince Adad-shuma-usur on the throne. The city is its own again.
ev.ane_h_adad_shuma_usur.note: Around 1216 BC the Babylonians threw off Assyrian rule; Adad-shuma-usur reigned for about 30 years. The dates are approximate.
ev.ane_h_sea_peoples.fight.success: The invaders were thrown back into the sea. You are alive and have spoils.
ev.ane_h_sea_peoples.fight.failure: You were badly wounded in the fighting at the river mouth.
ev.ane_h_sea_peoples.title: The Sea Peoples
ev.ane_h_sea_peoples.text: Whole peoples are coming from the north, by ship and in ox-carts with their families. They say they have already burned Ugarit and ravaged Hatti. Ramesses III is gathering an army and a fleet at the mouths of the Nile.
ev.ane_h_sea_peoples.note: In year 8 of Ramesses III (around 1177 BC) Egypt repelled an attack by the "Sea Peoples" — the Peleset, Tjeker, Sherden and others. The battle is shown at the temple of Medinet Habu. In the same decades the Hittite kingdom, Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces collapsed.
ev.ane_h_strike.join.success: A few days later the rations were issued. You won.
ev.ane_h_strike.join.failure: The rations came, but you were marked down as a ringleader.
ev.ane_h_strike.title: The strike
ev.ane_h_strike.text: The royal tomb workmen have downed tools: their rations are almost two months late. They sit by the memorial temples and shout: "We are hungry! No clothes, no oil, no fish!" The scribes run back and forth to the vizier.
ev.ane_h_strike.note: In year 29 of Ramesses III (around 1157/1155 BC) the workmen of Deir el-Medina stopped work several times over unpaid rations. It is the first documented strike in history (the Turin Strike Papyrus).
ev.ane_h_elam.stay.failure: The house was looted and you were beaten.
ev.ane_h_elam.title: The Elamites
ev.ane_h_elam.text: The Elamite king Shutruk-Nakhunte has swept through the land with fire. Ancient sacred objects are being carried off to Susa — even King Hammurabi's stela of laws. They say the Kassite dynasty is finished.
ev.ane_h_elam.note: Around 1158 BC the Elamites ravaged Babylonia and took Hammurabi's law stela to Susa, where archaeologists found it in 1901. Around 1155 BC the last Kassite king was overthrown.
ev.ane_h_harem_plot.title: The harem conspiracy
ev.ane_h_harem_plot.text: Rumours are creeping through the land: one of the wives of Ramesses III, Tiye, conspired with servants and officials to kill the king and put her son on the throne. They say the plotters even used wax figurines for sorcery. A trial is under way.
ev.ane_h_harem_plot.note: The conspiracy against Ramesses III is known from court papyri. A study of his mummy in 2012 showed that the king's throat had been cut. Tiye's son Pentawer and many plotters were condemned.
ev.ane_h_robbery_trials.testify.success: Your testimony helped the court, and the vizier noticed you.
ev.ane_h_robbery_trials.testify.failure: The people you named turned out to have protectors.
ev.ane_h_robbery_trials.title: The tomb-robbery trials
ev.ane_h_robbery_trials.text: The mayor of eastern Thebes has accused the mayor of the west bank of protecting the robbers of royal tombs. The vizier has convened a commission; stonecutters are questioned under the stick. Everyone fears being named.
ev.ane_h_robbery_trials.note: In year 16 of Ramesses IX (around 1110 BC) the robbery of royal tombs was investigated; the records survive in the Abbott and Amherst papyri. The robber Amenpanufer confessed to breaking into the tomb of King Sobekemsaf.
ev.ane_h_nebuchadnezzar.go.success: You came back with Marduk's army.
ev.ane_h_nebuchadnezzar.go.failure: The heat and the Elamite arrows nearly killed you.
ev.ane_h_nebuchadnezzar.title: Marduk home again
ev.ane_h_nebuchadnezzar.text: King Nebuchadnezzar led his army against Elam in the height of summer, defeated the Elamite king at the river Ulai and brought home the statue of Marduk, taken away many years before. The city rejoices.
ev.ane_h_nebuchadnezzar.note: Nebuchadnezzar I (around 1125–1104 BC) of the Second Dynasty of Isin defeated Elam and recovered the statue of Marduk. An inscription says the heat made "the roads burn like fire" and horses collapsed.
ev.ane_h_tiglath_pileser.go.success: You came back with spoils and captives.
ev.ane_h_tiglath_pileser.title: The Arameans
ev.ane_h_tiglath_pileser.text: King Tiglath-Pileser is leading the army across the Euphrates against the Arameans again — nomads who raid the fields and caravans. They say he has crossed the river more times than anyone can count, and still they come back.
ev.ane_h_tiglath_pileser.note: Tiglath-Pileser I (around 1114–1076 BC) wrote that he crossed the Euphrates 28 times campaigning against the Arameans. He also reached the Mediterranean.
ev.ane_h_famine_1080.hills: Go to the hills for food
ev.ane_h_famine_1080.title: The hungry years
ev.ane_h_famine_1080.text: One failed harvest after another, and the Arameans roam the roads taking the last of everything. People are leaving for the hills in search of food. Barley costs so much that silver won't buy a sack.
ev.ane_h_famine_1080.note: Later chronicles report a terrible famine and Aramean invasion in the last years of Tiglath-Pileser I (around 1082 BC). Cooler, drier climate across the Near East may have played a part. The dates and scale are disputed.
ev.ane_h_hyenas.title: The year of the hyenas
ev.ane_h_hyenas.text: Famine. The granaries are empty, Libyan bands roam near the west bank, and work in the Valley of the Kings has almost stopped. People call it "the year of the hyenas, when everyone went hungry".
ev.ane_h_hyenas.note: The phrase "the year of the hyenas, when there was hunger" occurs in Theban papyri from the end of the reign of Ramesses XI. It was a time of famine, unrest and tomb robbery; the exact date is unknown.
ev.ane_h_renaissance.temple: Stand by the temple of Amun
ev.ane_h_renaissance.title: "The Repeating of Births"
ev.ane_h_renaissance.text: After the turmoil, when the Nubian viceroy Panehsy lorded it over Thebes, power has been taken by the general and high priest of Amun, Herihor. A new era is proclaimed: the "Repeating of Births". The king is far away in the Delta; here a priest rules.
ev.ane_h_renaissance.note: In year 19 of Ramesses XI (around 1080 BC) the era of "wehem mesut" was proclaimed. The Theban high priests Herihor and Piankh effectively ruled Upper Egypt. The chronology of these years is disputed.
